evidence: Cic. Sen. 63: quae videntur levia atque commūnia
terms.comment: First “light in weight” (against gravis); figuratively “of no weight”, unimportant, trivial, and of persons fickle, unreliable (Lewis & Short). Not to be confused with lēvis, “smooth”, with a long e.

terms.grammar: phrase: genitive of quality; also parvī mōmentī, magnī mōmentī
evidence: Cic. Vatin. 1: nūllīus mōmentī aliquid putāre (Lewis & Short)
Caes. BG 7.39: levī mōmentō aestimāre (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: Mōmentum is the weight that tips a balance; so a thing of no, little or great moment. See important.

evidence: Ov. Tr. 2.214: sunt nōtitiā multa minōra tuā (Lewis & Short, s.v. parvus)
terms.comment: A true comparative, “smaller, less”: of age, younger (minor nātū, see younger); of rank, inferior. “Too trivial for” is minor with the ablative, as in Ovid. English “minor” as a plain adjective is usually levis or parvus (see small).

phrases.latin: haec enim ipsa sunt honōrābilia quae videntur levia atque commūnia
phrases.english: for these very things, which seem slight and ordinary, are marks of honour

sources: Lewis & Short: levis · Lewis & Short: momentum · Lewis & Short: parvus
